title: Hajime_Botnet_Investigation_314
description: Investigate and identify malicious activity in a network experiencing unusual traffic patterns.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: The network has experienced unusual traffic patterns and potential security incidents. Your task is to investigate and identify any malicious activity related to the Hajime botnet family, a known IoT malware that spreads via exploitation of default credentials and establishes persistence through systemd timers. Determine its scope and recommend containment measures. This training will guide you through the process of identifying suspicious services, excessive network traffic, and persistence mechanisms.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content: You have SSH access to the victim host `victim` with the username `ubuntu` and password `ubuntu`. From there, you can investigate the network and connected devices. Enter the word 'start' to progress to the next level.
levels.local_content: You have SSH access to the victim host `victim` with the username `ubuntu` and password `ubuntu`. From there, you can investigate the network and connected devices. Enter the word 'start' to progress to the next level.

levels.title: Identify Suspicious Service
levels.content:
Identify and investigate an unauthorized or suspicious service responsible for periodic external communication.

**Question:** What is the name of the suspicious service that is beaconing to an external host?
levels.solution: Check running services and look for any unusual network connections or periodic activities. The suspicious service is likely named `bot-beacon.service`.

hints.title: Conceptual Guidance
hints.content: Start by understanding the typical behavior of malicious services in a botnet context. Malicious services often communicate periodically with external hosts.

hints.title: Intermediate Hint
hints.content: Look for services that are scheduled to run periodically using systemd timers. Use the command `systemctl list-timers --all` to identify these services.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: Use the command `systemctl list-timers --all` to identify services that are scheduled to run periodically. Look for any unusual or unfamiliar service names.

levels.title: Identify Excessive Traffic Service
levels.content:
Identify the service responsible for generating abnormal volumes of network traffic.

**Question:** What is the name of the service generating excessive network traffic?
levels.solution: Examine network connections and look for services that are sending a high volume of packets to a specific destination. The service generating excessive network traffic is likely named `bot-flood.service`.

hints.title: Conceptual Guidance
hints.content: Consider how botnets typically generate excessive network traffic to overwhelm targets. Look for services with high network activity.

hints.title: Intermediate Hint
hints.content: Use network monitoring tools to identify services with high network activity. Commands like `netstat -tuln` or `ss -tuln` can help you identify these services.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: Use the command `netstat -tuln` or `ss -tuln` to identify services with high network activity. Look for services with a high number of connections or data transfer.

levels.title: Determine Persistence Mechanism
levels.content:
Determine how the suspicious service is automatically started after reboot.

**Question:** What is the persistence mechanism used by the suspicious service?
levels.solution: Investigate systemd services and timers to find how the service is scheduled to run periodically. The persistence mechanism is likely a systemd timer named `bot-beacon.timer`.

hints.title: Conceptual Guidance
hints.content: Understand how malware often uses systemd timers to maintain persistence. Look for timers that trigger the suspicious service.

hints.title: Intermediate Hint
hints.content: Look for systemd timers that trigger the suspicious service. Use the command `systemctl list-timers --all` to identify these timers.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: Use the command `systemctl list-timers --all` to look for systemd timers that trigger the suspicious service. Look for any unusual or unfamiliar timer names.
